name: Giziga, northern dialect

Leiden: Brill. doi:10.1163/9789004445970 (ch. 1 'The Giziga Language' pp. 1-16; ch. 2 'Phonology' pp. 17-65, doi:10.1163/9789004445970_003). Corroborated by Lukas, Johannes. 1970. Les relations lexicales entre le giziga – tchadique central – et le fulfulde (Cameroun). Afrika und Ubersee 98(1): 98-135, p. 103.
catalog_locator: Shay 2021 via Google Books feed (volume sI8cEAAAQBAJ; the feed gives no page numbers): noun overview in ch. 1 (pp. 1-16) and the vowel-reduction passage with example (7) in ch. 2 'Phonology' (pp. 17-65); saved excerpts: default final stress; closed-syllable generalization with the Lukas 1970: 19-20 cross-reference; mívìŋ 'door', ex. (7); two-tone system, stress and intonation. Lukas 1970 via volume H1W5AAAAIAAJ, Tourneux & Michielan 2025 p. 103 full text in the copy consulted.
catalog_quote: The default position for stress in the noun stem is the final syllable. In bisyllabic and polysyllabic noun stems, the placement of stress is correlated with vowel quality: A stressed syllable has a full vowel, while a vowel in an unstressed syllable can be centralized or even omitted in rapid speech. ... polysyllabic noun ending in a closed syllable, the stress is on the final syllable. This generalization is based on auditory evidence and is supported by the fact that the final closed syllable has a full vowel while an earlier vowel in the stem can be reduced or even deleted (see also Lukas (1970): 19-20 for correlations between stress and vowel quality). In mívìŋ 'door' (mí 'mouth' vì 'room'), the stress is on the final syllable and the vowel of the initial syllable can be reduced: (7) ... ... Giziga tone system, which involves two underlying tones, High and Low. These sections describe the grammatical and lexical functions of tone and posit interactions between tone and other prosodic means, including stress and intonation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Le fulfulde est une langue sans tons, alors que le giziga a deux registres tonals (haut et bas). Nos sources giziga ne notent malheureusement pas les tons, sauf à de très rares exceptions.
new_statements.translation: Fulfulde is a language without tones, whereas Giziga has two tonal registers (high and low). Unfortunately our Giziga sources do not mark the tones, except in very rare cases.
new_statements.citation: Tourneux, Henry & Antonio Michielan. 2025. Les relations lexicales entre le giziga – tchadique central – et le fulfulde (Cameroun). Afrika und Übersee 98(1): 98–135. doi:10.15460/auue.2025.98.1.332
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again., p. 7 = printed p. 103, §2.5 'Comparaison des deux systèmes' (extracted text): "Le fulfulde est une langue sans tons, alors que le giziga a deux registres tonals (haut et bas). Nos sources giziga ne notent malheu-reusement pas les tons, sauf à de très rares exceptions." Verbatim; only difference is the line-break hyphen in 'malheureusement'. §2 (pp. 100-103) is a consonant/vowel inventory summary after Shay 2021: 17-28; a full-text search for stress/accent all four copies we hold for accent/stress/prosod/Akzent/Betonung finds nothing about word stress. So the compilers account of the copies we hold is accurate. WHY THE READING AND STATUS CHANGE: the decisive…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress placement is given by any source opened. Giziga is described as a two-register tone language (H, L); Njui & Bebey 2021: 226 add a surface Mid tone and HL falling contours. Neither open source mentions word stress or accent at all; the 49-page phonology chapter of Shay 2021 (pp. 17–65), the only full modern description, could not be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the article's own lexical sources do not mark tone.
new_statements.domain_note: General statement about the language; the article's data are a lexicon (Michielan et al. ms., built on René Jaouen's file for giziga-sud/Muturwa) and its phonology summary follows Shay 2021: 17–28.
new_statements.identity_note: Shay 2021 and Lukas 1970 treat North (Dogba/Maroua, nort3047) and South (Muturwa, sout3051) Giziga as one language, and Glottolog cites Shay 2021 on both pages while listing the dialect 'Muturuwa' [mutu1250] under North Giziga; per Tourneux & Michielan 2025: 98–99 Lukas's description centres on the northern Dogba variety. The tone statement quoted comes from Tourneux & Michielan, whose lexical data derive from René Jaouen's giziga-sud (Muturwa) file and whose phonology summary follows Shay 2021, so it applies to Giziga as a whole rather than specifically to North Giziga. Njui & Bebey 2021 (Univ. of Maroua) do not name their variety.

tone_statements.quote: C'est d'une langue du Nord-Cameroun que traite l'ouvrage du Prof. Lukas, Studien zur Sprache der Gisiga. ... Le corps de l'ouvrage suit une présentation très classique et consacre d'abord une première partie aux faits articulatoires. D'abord à la phonologie, caractérisée comme celle du mandara par un système consonantique développé en regard d'un vocalisme réduit à trois unités pertinentes (contre deux en mandara), puis la prosodie présentant un jeu de trois tons ponctuels et de deux tons modulés.
tone_statements.translation: It is a language of North Cameroon that Prof. Lukas's book, Studien zur Sprache der Gisiga, deals with. ... The body of the work follows a very classical presentation and first devotes a first part to articulatory facts. First to the phonology, characterised like that of Mandara by a developed consonant system against a vowel system reduced to three distinctive units (against two in Mandara), then the prosody, presenting a set of three level (punctual) tones and two modulated (contour) tones.
tone_statements.summary: Reviewer's summary of Lukas 1970: Gisiga prosody has three level ('ponctuels') tones and two contour ('modulés') tones; the tones are not named and nothing more is said.

sources.note: §2 'Les systèmes phonologiques du giziga et du fulfulde' (pp. 100–103) gives consonant and vowel inventories after Shay (2021: 17–28) and states on p. 103 that Giziga has two tone registers (high, low); nothing whatsoever on stress or accent. Also states (p. 98) that Lukas 1970, Barreteau & Dieu 2000 and Shay 2021 treat North and South Giziga as one language, and that Lukas's work centred on the Dogba (northern) variety.
